look_here_first: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS (maygrass): look for a fairly firm, dense, oval-to-elongate light-green head with overlapping pointed, faintly green-and-pale-striped glumes, above flat shiny leaves on an ANNUAL grass. The true test is ONE dissected 4–6 mm spikelet: two narrow, hairy REDUCED STERILE florets below one fertile floret, surrounded by two keeled, narrowly winged glumes. Introduced lesser canarygrass (Phalaris minor) has ONE reduced sterile floret; head shape, flowering color and site moisture are insufficient by themselves.

best_field_traits: Annual fibrous-rooted, usually several erect/ascending tillers (not a persistent rhizomatous Phalaris colony).
Panicle dense and spikelike, often ovoid to subcylindrical, about 0.5–8 cm long and 0.8–2 cm wide; green, pale-striped overlapping outer glumes, awnless.

Spikelets strongly flattened side to side, about 3.8–6 mm; two similar sharply keeled glumes with narrow distal wings, typically entire; do not label individual wing edges from an unmeasured group photo.
Decisive mature dissection: TWO hairy reduced sterile florets roughly 1.5–2.5 mm long plus ONE fertile floret, unlike P. minor's ONE reduced sterile floret.
True leaf ligule is a translucent membrane, often 1.5–7 mm, best measured in a sharp collar macro; no reliable photo of this structure yet.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full rooted spring grass with fibrous annual roots, multiple leafy culms, intact seedhead and an actual ruler
Same-shoot leaf sheath/blade junction showing pale membranous ligule measured with 1-mm scale
One mature detached and OPENED Phalaris caroliniana spikelet, both lateral sides, individually labeled two narrow sterile lemmas and fertile floret with scale
Compare to a confirmed P. minor spikelet with exactly ONE sterile lemma and toothed/erose glume wing in matching magnification
Mat-like fluffy Polypogon monspeliensis foxtail head, with visible awns contrasted against the layered Phalaris head (no false counts from distant photographs)
crew_field_check: At first glance look for a tight green, firm, rather ovoid canarygrass seedhead with sharp overlapping glumes instead of the longer fluffy awn-bearing bottlebrush of Polypogon.
Locate the entire plant base and collar: Carolina canarygrass is a cool-season annual with a membranous ligule; season and damp site are supporting, not decisive.
Separate P. minor from P. caroliniana at magnification by counting reduced STERILE FLORETS inside ONE opened spikelet: ONE in introduced P. minor versus TWO in Carolina canarygrass.
Check P. canariensis: another introduced annual with TWO sterile florets but considerably broader conspicuous glume wings and often larger glumes; do not confuse broad wing with the sterile lemmas.

Check narrow panicles against native P. angusta (two shorter reduced florets, generally narrower cylindrical panicle) and rhizomatous perennial P. arundinacea; both require site/range verification and dissection.
Do not reclassify unknown canarygrass as native based on one photo, nor change Hays county nativity metrics.

comparisons.key_distinctions: P. minor is the dangerous look-alike: similarly firm compact canarygrass head, usually one sterile floret (vs two in Carolina); P. minor's glume wings are often irregularly dentate, Carolina usually smoother/entire but variable. P. canariensis ALSO has two sterile florets: its glumes are markedly broader, typically 7–10 mm, with more obvious wings. P. angusta is generally more narrowly cylindrical and has shorter reduced sterile florets (~0.7–1.5 mm vs Carolina 1.5–2.5 mm). Polypogon monspeliensis has fine long awns giving a soft fuzzy head. P. arundinacea is perennial/rhizomatous with potentially spreading flowering branches; annual rooted base confirms against that species.

visual_comparison.title: CAROLINA CANARYGRASS — recognize the head, then count sterile florets
visual_comparison.subtitle: 3 credited real-source photo panels: 1 existing archived Carolina head, 1 NEW external Carolina leaf-and-head view, 1 NEW clearly labelled DIFFERENT SPECIES P. minor comparison. 7 visible gross-feature arrows. Inner sterile florets remain unphotographed.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: CAROLINA: TWO reduced sterile florets + one fertile inside paired keeled glumes. MINOR: ONE reduced sterile floret. The green dense head is a clue, NOT confirmation.

items.label: DIFFERENT SPECIES — Phalaris minor head with overlapping pointed glumes
items.image_role: True source-labelled, publicly CC BY licensed Phalaris minor flowering-head comparison from Australia. NOT Carolina canarygrass and not a Texas specimen.
items.caption: This introduced lesser canarygrass ALSO makes a dense, green, layered canarygrass head and can expose dark-purple anthers. The similarity is the lesson: dissect an actual individual spikelet before using this as P. caroliniana. Lesser canarygrass generally has ONE sterile floret, Carolina TWO; that diagnostic difference is NOT visible in this full-head photograph.
items.why_it_matters: Stops the crew from claiming every green pointed canarygrass head is native maygrass; the verified species-level key is the reduced sterile-floret count, not anther color.
